front: Visual metaphor: I/O management is like the shipping department of a toy shop. What three parallels does the lecture draw?
back:
• Protocols: the shop has protocols for how parts come in and orders ship out; the OS has interfaces per device type that determine the protocols used to access those devices.
  • Dedicated handlers: the shop has dedicated shipping staff; the OS has device drivers and interrupt handlers dedicated to accessing and interacting with devices.
  • Decoupled I/O details: making toys is separate from the details of shipping; through its interfaces and device driver model, the OS hides device details from applications and from the upper levels of the system software stack.

front: I/O devices: what are they, and give three examples.
back: Hardware components tied to receiving inputs or directing outputs. Examples: keyboards, microphones, displays, speakers, mice, network interface cards, hard disks.

front: I/O devices quiz: classify keyboard, microphone, speaker, display, hard disk drive, NIC, and flash card as input, output, or both.
back:
• Input: keyboards, microphones.
  • Output: speakers, displays.
  • Both: hard disk drives, network interface cards (NICs), flash cards.

front: Device control registers: what three register types let the CPU interact with a device, and what is each for?
back:
• Command registers: CPU uses to control the device.
  • Data registers: CPU uses to transfer data in and out of the device.
  • Status registers: CPU reads to understand what is happening on the device.

front: Device internals: what components does a device have internally, and what is the microcontroller?
back: Internally a device has a microcontroller (the device's own CPU), on-device memory, and other device-specific logic, e.g. chips for converting analog to digital signals, or chips for network devices to interact with the physical medium (optics or copper wire).

front: CPU/device interconnect: how do controllers typically connect to the rest of the system?
back: Each device interfaces via a controller integrated into its packaging, which connects to the CPU complex over a CPU/device interconnect such as the PCI (Peripheral Component Interconnect) bus.

front: PCI Express vs PCI-X/PCI: how is it better, and why do platforms still include PCI-X?
back: PCI Express has more bandwidth, is faster, has lower latency, and supports more devices. For compatibility, platforms still include PCI-X (PCI extended), the follow-on to the original PCI standard, because it is compatible with PCI.

front: Interconnects: besides PCI, name two other buses a system may have and what they connect.
back: A SCSI bus connects SCSI disks, and an expansion (peripheral) bus connects things like keyboards.

front: Interconnects: what determines which interconnect a device attaches to, and what handles differences between interconnect types?
back: The device controller determines what interconnect a device can attach to. Bridging controllers handle differences between different types of interconnects.

front: Device drivers: what are they and what are they responsible for?
back: Device-specific software components. The OS needs one for every type of device in the system. They are responsible for all aspects of device access, management, and control, including how requests pass to the device and how to respond to errors and notifications.

front: Device drivers: who is responsible for providing them?
back: The device manufacturer is responsible for making drivers available for all operating systems where the device will be used (e.g. downloading printer drivers from HP).

front: Device driver frameworks: why do operating systems standardize their interface to device drivers?
back: To decouple the OS from a fixed set of specific devices. Manufacturers develop drivers within the framework; switching a hardware component only requires switching its driver, and the rest of the OS and the applications are unaffected. The OS achieves device independence (it need not be specialized for each device) and device diversity (it can support arbitrarily different types of devices: it just needs another driver).

front: Block devices: what granularity do they operate at, and what key access property do they have?
back: They operate at the granularity of blocks of data delivered to and from the device via the CPU interconnect. Key property: individual blocks can be accessed directly (you can request the ninth of ten blocks directly). Example: disks.

front: Character devices: what do they work with and what interface do they support?
back: They work with a serial sequence of characters and support a get/put character interface. Example: keyboards.

front: Network devices: how do they fit between block and character devices?
back: They deliver more than a character at a time, but their granularity is not a fixed block size. They are more like a stream of data chunks of potentially different sizes.

text: The device interface exposed to the OS is standardized by device type: all block devices support {{c1::reading and writing}} a block of data, and all character devices support operations to {{c2::get and put a character}}.

front: Device representation: how does the OS internally represent each device, and why?
back: Using a file abstraction where each file represents a device. This lets the OS interact with devices via the same interface it already maintains for files, though operations are handled in a device-specific manner.

front: UNIX-like systems: where do devices appear and which filesystems treat them?
back: All devices appear as files under the /dev directory. They are special files, not stored on the real filesystem, treated by the special filesystems tmpfs and devfs.

front: I/O devices as files quiz: three Linux commands write content (a file, or "Hello, world") into /dev/lp0. What do they do, and what does lp0 mean?
back: All three perform the same operation: they print to the lp0 printer device. lp stands for line printer, and 0 is the first line printer identified by the system.

front: Pseudo devices quiz: which Linux pseudo device discards all output, and which produces pseudo-random numbers (plus its more robust counterpart)?
back:
Pseudo (virtual) devices do not represent actual hardware.
  • /dev/null: accepts and discards all output without producing anything (e.g. to discard a process's output).
  • /dev/random: produces a variable-length string of pseudo-random numbers; /dev/urandom is its more robust counterpart, used e.g. to create files of pseudo-random bytes.

front: Looking at /dev quiz: what do the device names hda/sda, tty, null, and lp represent?
back:
• hda or sda: drives, like hard drives, SSDs, or CD-ROMs.
  • tty: terminal stations, usable to pipe output to and from terminals.
  • null: the null device.
  • lp: printers.

front: Memory-mapped I/O: how do device registers appear to the CPU, and what controls the reserved region?
back: Device registers appear as memory locations at specific physical addresses; the integrated PCI controller routes those accesses to the device. A portion of physical memory is dedicated to device interactions (memory-mapped I/O), and the reserved region is controlled by the Base Address Registers (BAR), which determine how much memory, starting at which address, a particular device uses; they are configured at boot per the PCI protocol.

front: I/O Port Model: how does the CPU access devices with special instructions?
back: x86 platforms specify in/out instructions for accessing devices. Each instruction specifies the target device (the I/O port) and a value stored in registers: the value to be written out to the device or the value read from the device.

front: Device-to-CPU path: what are the two routes information can take from device to CPU?
back:
• The device generates an interrupt to the CPU.
  • The CPU polls the device by reading its status registers to determine if it has a response/data.

front: Interrupts: what is the main downside and the main benefit?
back: Downside: the interrupt handler costs CPU cycles (handler steps, setting/resetting interrupt masks, and indirect effects like cache pollution). Benefit: interrupts can be triggered by the device as soon as it has information for the CPU.

front: Polling: what is the main benefit and the main downsides?
back: Benefit: the OS chooses when to poll, so it can poll when cache pollution is lowest. Downsides: it can delay how an event is observed or handled (handling happens after the event is generated), and too much polling may add unaffordable CPU overhead.

front: Interrupts vs polling: what factors decide which is better?
back: It depends on the device and objectives: whether optimizing for throughput or latency, how complex the interrupt handling routine is, and the device's load characteristics such as its input and output data rates.

front: Programmed I/O (PIO): what hardware support does it need and how does the CPU drive the device?
back: It requires no extra hardware support beyond a basic interconnect like PCI. The CPU issues instructions by writing to the device's command registers and controls data movement by reading/writing the device's data registers.

front: PIO NIC example: how many CPU accesses to transmit a 1500B packet with 8B data registers, and how is that computed?
back: 189 CPU accesses: 1 access to the command register plus 188 to the data register (1500 / 8 rounded up = 188). Each access is a CPU store instruction.

front: Direct Memory Access (DMA): what hardware does it need and how does data movement differ from PIO?
back: It requires a DMA controller. The CPU still writes commands to the device's command registers, but data movement is controlled by configuring the DMA controller with which data to move between memory and the device.

front: DMA NIC example: how many operations to transmit a 1500B packet with 8B data registers?
back: 2 operations: 1 CPU access to the command register plus 1 DMA configuration operation (which also tells the DMA controller the memory address and size of the packet buffer).

front: DMA vs PIO: why is PIO still better for small transfers?
back: DMA configuration is not trivial; it takes many more cycles than a memory access. For smaller transfers, PIO is more efficient than paying the DMA configuration cost.

front: DMA pinned memory: why must the DMA data buffer stay in physical memory, and what is that called?
back: The DMA controller only has access to physical memory, so the buffer cannot be swapped out to disk until the transfer completes. Such regions are pinned (non-swappable).

front: DMA vs PIO quiz: store = 1 cycle, DMA config = 5 cycles, 8B bus. Which wins for a keyboard, and which for a NIC?
back: For a keyboard (little data per keystroke) PIO wins, since one or two stores are cheaper than configuring DMA. For a NIC it depends on transfer size: packets needing fewer than five stores favor PIO; larger transfers favor DMA.

front: Typical device access: list the chain from user process to device for an operation.
back:
1. User process makes a system call for the operation.
  2. OS runs the in-kernel stack for the device, possibly preprocessing data (e.g. forming a TCP/IP packet).
  3. OS invokes the device driver, which configures the request to the device.
  4. The driver issues commands and data via PIO or DMA.
  5. The device performs the actual request.
Results/events traverse the chain in reverse: device to driver to kernel to user process.

front: Typical device access: when issuing PIO/DMA operations, what must the driver ensure about commands and data?
back: The driver ensures that any commands and data needed by the device are not overwritten or undelivered.

front: Typical device access, disk read: what do the kernel stack, the driver, and the device each do?
back:
• Kernel stack: the filesystem determines the particular disk block that stores the file data.
  • Driver: issues commands to the disk that configure the disk head movement and where the data should be read from.
  • Device: the disk performs the block read operation.

front: OS bypass: what is it and what is directly available to the user process?
back: Configuring some devices to be accessible directly from user level, without going through the kernel. Any memory/registers assigned for use by the device are directly available to the user process. The OS is involved in configuring this, making sure the device's registers and memory are mapped into the user process, then stays out of the way.

front: OS bypass: what replaces the kernel driver, and who provides it?
back: A user-level driver (a library) that the user process links to interact with the device. Like kernel drivers, these libraries are usually provided by the device manufacturers.

front: OS bypass: what coarse-grain control does the OS retain, and what must the device have for that?
back: The OS can still enable/disable the device or add permissions for more processes to use it. The device must have enough registers so the OS can map some into user processes while retaining a few for its own high-level interaction.

front: OS bypass: when is it not possible, and how can one device be shared by multiple processes?
back: It is not possible if the device has too few registers and reuses the same registers for both data movement and control operations. With enough registers, different subsets can be assigned to different user processes, so the same device is shared across multiple processes.

front: OS bypass: who performs demultiplexing of data to the right process, and how does this differ from the normal case?
back: Normally the kernel demultiplexes incoming data to the right process. In OS bypass, that responsibility is left to the device itself, which must figure out which process each chunk of data belongs to. E.g. for a received network packet, the device peeks at the destination port number and must know which socket port numbers the processes use; those checks move from the kernel to the device.

front: Synchronous I/O: what happens to the calling thread?
back: The thread blocks. The kernel places it on the wait queue associated with the device, and it becomes runnable again when the response to its request is available.

front: Asynchronous I/O: what are the two ways the process learns its request completed?
back: Either the process later checks whether the response is available, or the kernel notifies the process that the operation is complete and the results are available.

front: Async I/O: what does kernel notification of completion save the process, and what is it analogous to?
back: With notification the process does not have to check periodically whether the results are available. This is analogous to interrupts versus polling.

front: Block device stack: what is a file, logically vs physically?
back: A file is a logical storage unit that maps to some underlying physical storage location. User processes think in files, not in blocks of storage.

front: Block device stack: what does the filesystem do with a read/write for a file?
back: It receives the operation from the user process and has the information to find the file, determine if the process can access it, and which portion to access. The filesystem then ultimately initiates the actual access.

front: Block device stack: what standardized API lets filesystems be swapped without breaking applications?
back: The POSIX API, which includes the read, write, and open system calls. Standardizing this interface lets a filesystem be modified or replaced without breaking user applications. OSes also standardize how filesystems interact with the underlying storage devices and with other OS components.

front: Generic block layer: what problem does it solve and what does it provide?
back: Different block devices need protocol-specific APIs and differ, for instance in the types of errors they report and how they report them. The generic block layer masks these differences by providing a standard interface for the OS to all types of block devices, so the filesystem sees one consistent block API; the full device features remain accessible through the device driver.

front: Block device stack: name the layers from application down to device.
back:
1. Application (file interface, POSIX API)
  2. Filesystem
  3. Generic block layer
  4. Device driver
  5. Block device
The filesystem gives user processes a consistent file API; the OS gives the filesystem a consistent block API.

front: Block device stack: trace a file read through the layers. What does each layer do?
back:
1. The user process invokes read or write on a file through the POSIX API.
  2. The kernel-level filesystem determines the exact device and the exact block on it that holds that region of the file.
  3. Generic read block / write block operations go to the generic block layer, which knows how to pass them to the particular driver and how to interpret the driver's error messages, notifications, and responses.
  4. The driver handles lower-level differences among devices, such as their protocols, and speaks the device's specific protocol.

front: Virtual File System (VFS): what three motivating problems does it solve?
back:
• Seeing files across multiple devices as a single coherent filesystem.
  • Different device types working better with different filesystem implementations.
  • Files that are not local, accessed over the network.

front: VFS: what does it hide, what API do applications keep using, and what does it require of filesystems?
back: It hides all details of the underlying filesystem(s) from higher-level consumers. Applications keep using the same POSIX API, and the VFS specifies filesystem abstractions that every underlying filesystem must implement.

front: VFS: what is a file descriptor?
back: An integer created when a file is first opened. Many operations can be performed on a file via its descriptor, such as read, write, locking the file, sendfile, and close.

front: VFS inode: what does it maintain and why is it called the "index node"?
back: The inode is a persistent per-file data structure that maintains the list of all data blocks for the file, so it is the file's index node. It also holds metadata like permissions, size, and whether the file is locked. It matters because files need not be stored contiguously; blocks may be scattered across the media.

front: VFS: how does the VFS treat a directory?
back: A directory is itself just a file. Its contents are information about the files it holds and their inodes, which the VFS interprets to locate the data blocks for those files.

front: VFS dentry: what does a dentry correspond to, and give the example for /users/ada.
back: A dentry (directory entry) corresponds to a single path component being traversed. For /users/ada the filesystem creates a dentry for /, /users, and /users/ada.

front: VFS dentry cache: what does it store, and are dentries persisted?
back: It contains directories previously visited, so re-reading the entire path is unnecessary when finding another file in an already-visited directory. The dentry cache is soft state: dentry objects live only in memory and have no persistent on-disk representation.

front: VFS superblock: what does it provide?
back: Information about how a particular filesystem is laid out on a storage device. It maintains a map the filesystem uses to figure out how it organized persistent elements like inodes and data blocks, plus filesystem-specific metadata (which varies by filesystem).

text: Of the VFS abstractions, {{c1::dentries}} live only in memory and are not persisted, while files, inodes, and the superblock correspond to {{c2::blocks}} present on disk.

front: VFS on disk: what does the superblock's map let the filesystem distinguish, and what is it used for?
back: It maps all blocks on the device so the filesystem can tell which blocks hold data, which hold inodes, and which are free. The map is used for both allocation and lookup.

front: ext2: what was its role in Linux and what replaced it?
back: ext2 (Second Extended Filesystem) was the default filesystem in several versions of Linux until it was replaced by ext3 and ext4. It is not Linux specific; it is also available for other operating systems.

front: ext2 partition layout: what is the first block used for, and how is the rest divided?
back: The first block is not used by Linux and is often used to boot the system. The rest of the partition is divided into block groups (whose size has no correlation to the disk's physical geometry).

front: ext2 block group: what information does its super block contain?
back:
• Number of inodes.
  • Number of disk blocks.
  • Start of free blocks.

front: ext2 group descriptor: what does it contain, and why track the number of directories?
back: It contains the location of the bitmaps, the number of free inodes, and the number of directories. The number of directories is tracked because ext2 tries to balance the overall allocation of directories and files across block groups.

front: ext2 bitmaps: what are they used for?
back: To quickly find free blocks and inodes. Higher-level allocators read the bitmaps to easily determine which blocks and inodes are free and which are in use.

front: ext2 inode: how big is it, what does it describe, and what does it contain?
back: Every ext2 inode is a 128B data structure describing exactly one file. Inodes are numbered from 1 to some maximum. It contains file ownership, accounting information that system calls like stat return, and pointers to the actual data blocks.

front: inode indexing: what does an inode integrate, and what two access patterns does it make easy?
back: It integrates an index of all disk blocks for a file (plus metadata); a file is uniquely identified by its inode (inodes are uniquely numbered, so a file is identified by its inode number). The benefit is that both sequential and random accesses to the file are easy.

front: inode growth: how does the filesystem add storage to a file using a flat inode block list?
back: It allocates a free block and updates the inode to add another entry pointing to the newly allocated block (e.g. a sixth entry for a 5-block file).

front: inode block list: how are sequential and random access to a file performed?
back:
• Sequential: get the next index in the inode's list of blocks.
  • Random: compute from the block size which block reference is needed.

front: Flat inode block list: what is the downside, with the 128B inode example?
back: There is a limit on file size. A 128B inode with 4B block pointers addresses only 32 blocks (assuming it holds only block pointers, no metadata); at 1KB per block the file size limit is 32KB, which is too restrictive.

front: Indirect pointers: what does a single indirect pointer point to, and how much content with 1KB blocks and 4B pointers?
back: It points to a block of pointers, each of which points to data. With 1KB blocks and 4B pointers, a single indirect pointer addresses 256KB of file content.

front: Double indirect pointer: what does it point to and how much content can it address?
back: It points to a block of single indirect pointers, which point to pointers to data. A single double indirect pointer addresses 256 * 256 * 1KB = 64MB of file content.

front: Indirect pointers: what is the benefit and the downside?
back: Benefit: relatively small inodes can address really large files. Downside: file access is slowed. Without indirect pointers at most two disk accesses are needed (inode + block); with double indirect pointers the count doubles (inode + block + two pointers).

front: inode max file size quiz: with 12 direct + single + double + triple indirect pointers, 4B pointers and 1KB blocks, what is the max size, and what with 8KB blocks?
back: A triple indirect pointer points to a block of double indirect pointers. 256 pointers per block gives (12 + 256 + 256^2 + 256^3) * 1KB, rounding to 16GB. With 8KB blocks (2K pointers per block) the same structure reaches 64TB; increasing block size eightfold raises the limit far more than eightfold because the gain compounds through the indirect levels.

front: Buffer caches: how do they reduce disk accesses, and which system call flushes them?
back: Content is written to and read from caches in main memory and periodically flushed to disk, amortizing the cost of a disk access over multiple writes that hit the cache in between. The fsync system call supports flushing.

front: I/O scheduling: what is its main goal and how does it achieve it?
back: To reduce slow disk head movement, by maximizing sequential accesses over random accesses. For example, with the head at position 15 and requests for block 25 then block 17, it may reorder so it writes block 17 on the way to block 25 instead of backtracking.

front: Prefetching: what does it exploit, what does it do, and what is the tradeoff?
back: It exploits locality in file access by fetching nearby blocks during a request (e.g. reading blocks 18 and 19 when block 17 is requested). Tradeoff: it uses more disk bandwidth (three times as much in this example) but can significantly reduce access latency by raising the cache hit rate.

front: Journaling: what problem does it address and how does it work?
back: I/O scheduling keeps data in memory, so a crash loses those blocks. Instead of writing data to its proper (random) disk location immediately, journaling writes updates to a log describing the write (block, offset, content). The logged writes are periodically applied to proper disk locations so the log does not grow indefinitely.

front: Journaling: which filesystems use it?
back: The ext3 and ext4 filesystems, along with many others.

front: Disk access optimizations: name the four techniques and the three ways they reduce filesystem overheads and latencies.
back:
Caching (buffer caches), I/O scheduling, prefetching, and journaling. They help by:
  • increasing the likelihood of accessing data from memory;
  • not having to wait on slow disk head movements;
  • reducing the overall number of disk accesses, especially random ones.
